statement: Prove that a space X is Hausdorff if and only if the diagonal Δ = {(x,x)} is closed in X × X.
solution: (⇒) If X is Hausdorff and (x,y)∉Δ then x≠y; take disjoint opens U∋x, V∋y, so U×V is a neighborhood of (x,y) disjoint from Δ. Hence the complement of Δ is open. (⇐) If Δ is closed and x≠y, then (x,y) lies in the open complement, so some basic open U×V contains (x,y) and misses Δ; U×V∩Δ=∅ means U∩V=∅, so U,V are disjoint opens separating x and y.

statement: Prove that the order topology on R (from the usual order) coincides with the standard topology.
solution: The order topology has as basis the open intervals (a,b) together with the rays (-∞,b) and (a,∞). Each of these is open in the standard topology, and each standard basic interval (a,b) is an order-topology basic set. Rays are unions of bounded intervals, so the two topologies have inter-generating bases and hence are equal.

statement: Prove that any set with the finite-complement topology is compact.
solution: Let {U_i} be an open cover. Pick one nonempty U_0 from it; its complement X\U_0 is finite, say {x_1,...,x_n}. Choose U_1,...,U_n from the cover with x_k∈U_k. Then U_0,U_1,...,U_n is a finite subcover. Hence the space is compact.

statement: Prove that a retract of a Hausdorff space is closed. (A retract is the image of a continuous r: X → A ⊆ X with r restricted to A the identity.)
solution: The retraction r:X→X (viewed into X) and the identity are two continuous maps X→X. Their agreement set E={x: r(x)=x} is closed because X is Hausdorff (E is the preimage of the diagonal, closed by adv01, under x↦(r(x),x)). Since r|A=id and r(X)=A, we get E=A. Hence A is closed.

statement: Prove that R^n is locally compact.
solution: Every point x∈R^n lies in the closed ball of radius 1 about x, which is closed and bounded, hence compact by Heine-Borel, and is a neighborhood of x (it contains the open ball). So each point has a compact neighborhood, i.e. R^n is locally compact.

statement: Prove that the continuous image of a separable space is separable.
solution: Let f:X→Y be continuous with X separable via countable dense D, and consider f(X). Then f(D) is countable, and f(X)=f(cl(D))⊆cl(f(D)) by continuity (c12). So f(D) is a countable dense subset of f(X); hence f(X) is separable.

statement: Prove that a quotient space of a connected space is connected.
solution: A quotient map q:X→Y is a continuous surjection. The continuous image of a connected space is connected (cn-style / continuous image argument), and q(X)=Y, so Y is connected.

statement: State the Baire category theorem and the hypotheses it requires.
solution: Baire category theorem: in a complete metric space (or a locally compact Hausdorff space), the intersection of countably many dense open sets is dense; equivalently, such a space is not a countable union of nowhere-dense sets. Essential hypothesis: completeness of the metric (or local compactness + Hausdorff); it fails in general incomplete spaces such as Q.

statement: State the Urysohn metrization theorem and its hypotheses.
solution: Urysohn metrization theorem: every regular, second-countable space (equivalently, every regular Lindelof T1 space) is metrizable — it embeds homeomorphically into the Hilbert cube [0,1]^ω. Hypotheses: T3 (regular + T1) and second countability.

statement: State the Tietze extension theorem and its hypotheses.
solution: Tietze extension theorem: if X is normal and A⊆X is closed, then every continuous map f:A→R extends to a continuous map F:X→R (and any f:A→[a,b] extends to F:X→[a,b]). Hypotheses: X normal and A closed.

statement: Prove that the standard middle-thirds Cantor set is compact and totally disconnected.
solution: The Cantor set C=∩_n C_n, where each C_n is a finite union of closed intervals, hence closed; C is a closed subset of the compact space [0,1], so C is compact. Totally disconnected: for distinct x,y∈C, some removed middle-third gap (a,b) satisfies x<a<b<y up to relabeling and (a,b)∩C=∅, so C∩(-∞,a) and C∩(b,∞) separate x from y. Thus the only connected subsets are singletons.

statement: Prove that an open subspace of a locally compact Hausdorff space is locally compact.
solution: Let U be open in a locally compact Hausdorff X and x∈U. In an LCH space, x has a neighborhood basis of sets with compact closure; since U is open, choose an open V∋x with cl(V) compact and cl(V)⊆U (using regularity of LCH spaces). Then cl(V) is a compact neighborhood of x within U. Hence U is locally compact.

statement: Prove that connectedness is a topological invariant.
solution: Let h:X→Y be a homeomorphism. If X is connected, then Y=h(X) is a continuous image of a connected space, hence connected. Applying the argument to h^{-1} gives the converse. So X is connected iff Y is; connectedness is preserved by homeomorphism.

statement: Prove that an injective quotient map is a homeomorphism.
solution: A quotient map q:X→Y is a continuous surjection with: U⊆Y open iff q^{-1}(U) open. If q is also injective it is a bijection. For any open V⊆X, q^{-1}(q(V))=V (injectivity+surjectivity) is open, so q(V) is open; thus q is an open map, making q^{-1} continuous. A continuous open bijection is a homeomorphism.

statement: Prove that the product of two second-countable spaces is second countable.
solution: If {U_n} is a countable basis for X and {V_m} a countable basis for Y, then {U_n×V_m} is a countable collection of open boxes. Given an open set W⊆X×Y and (x,y)∈W, there is a basic box A×B⊆W with x∈A, y∈B; choose U_n with x∈U_n⊆A and V_m with y∈V_m⊆B, so (x,y)∈U_n×V_m⊆W. Hence {U_n×V_m} is a countable basis for X×Y.
